results.title: Gender Stereotypes and Entrepreneur Financing
results.content: Consistent with the existence of context-dependent stereotypes, I show that the unexplained share of the gender gap in equity financing increases up to 80% in male-dominated sectors, whereas it is not significantly different from zero in female-dominated sectors. My first finding is that female entrepreneurs are, on average, 22% less likely to use equity and VC funding than are their male peers after accounting for gender differences in human capital, motivations for founding a new business, and startups’ characteristics. I provide two pieces of evidence suggesting that unobserved characteristics affecting demand for equity financing and gender-specific selection into sectors are unlikely to explain why entrepreneurs are more likely to raise capital in gender-congruent sectors where they fit the representative gender. This evidence suggests that, unlike equity investors, banks evaluate male and female entrepreneurs similarly, relying on objective measures like credit scores and repayment capacity (Petersen and Rajan 1994; Berger and Udell 1995), rather than the entrepreneur’s profile, particularly in the early stages when uncertainty is high (Brooks et al.
